headline: House shelves Hegseth impeachment as oil slides on Iran hopes
briefing: The Republican-led House voted 211-204 to send the impeachment articles against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to committee, ending the effort until Democrats take over in January. Oil briefly fell below US$90 a barrel as Trump said the Iran war could end soon, which could ease gas prices and the inflation behind the Bank of Canada's October hike. In Ontario, the province named eight powerful regional chairs and faces criticism that Bill 140 would weaken residents' environmental rights.

stories.headline: Brent dips below US$90 as Trump says Iran war could end 'fairly soon'
stories.summary: Oil fell to its lowest level since August after Trump said renewed U.S. strikes on Iran are quite unlikely, though Tehran denies any talks are under way and the U.S. naval blockade stays.
stories.now: Brent crude briefly slipped below US$90 a barrel on Tuesday for the first time since August, after settling at US$91.61 on Monday following a drop of nearly 7%. It is now roughly 25% below its late-October peak above US$117, as analysts note crude flows through the region have almost returned to pre-war levels. The move followed Trump's meeting with Qatar's prime minister, after which he said the war could end fairly soon and new strikes look quite unlikely, while U.S. forces stay ready and the blockade continues. Iran's security council secretary Mohsen Rezaei says there are no negotiations with Washington. Turkey's intelligence chief said Qatar hopes to bring U.S. Vice-President JD Vance and Rezaei together in Doha next week, a claim not confirmed by either side.
stories.backstory: The U.S. and Israel began striking Iran on Feb. 28, and Iran choked traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, route for about a fifth of the world's oil. A June peace memorandum briefly reopened it but collapsed in July, and the U.S. imposed a blockade on Iranian shipping. Qatar gave Iran a new draft deal on Oct. 25. Trump has said the war will end soon, one way or the other.

timeline.event: U.S. and Israel begin striking Iran
June deal collapses; U.S. blockade begins
Qatar hands Iran a new draft deal
Qatar PM meets Trump; Brent falls ~7%

stories.why: Oil prices are the main driver of higher inflation in Canada and the U.S.; the October spike is why the Bank of Canada raised rates on Oct. 28.
stories.impact: Lower crude usually reaches GTA gas pumps within days, which would ease fuel and delivery costs. A failed deal or new attacks on shipping could quickly reverse the drop.

stories.headline: House shelves Hegseth impeachment in 211-204 vote
stories.summary: The Republican-led House voted 211-204 on Tuesday to send Rep. Thomas Massie's impeachment articles against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to the Judiciary Committee, effectively ending the effort in this Congress.
stories.now: The motion to refer the eight articles to committee passed 211-204, with Massie the only Republican voting with all Democrats against it. Referral means there will be no floor vote on impeachment before the current Congress ends in January. Hegseth called the push a farce and a political spectacle, and the Pentagon hailed the result. Massie, who is retiring after losing his primary, has said he will not file another resolution. Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said the vote is just the beginning, and Democrats take control of the House in January.
stories.backstory: Massie's articles centre on the Iran war, which he says has run more than 90 days without approval from Congress, and also cite operations in Venezuela and Yemen. He first filed them in the fall, but the House left early for the campaign. Democrats won the House in the Nov. 3 midterms and take control in January; their leader Hakeem Jeffries calls himself a hard yes on impeachment.

timeline.event: Jeffries says he is a hard yes

stories.why: The vote ends the impeachment push for now, but Democrats can revive it, or hold hearings on the Iran war, once they control the House in January. Removal would still need two-thirds of the Senate.
stories.impact: The effects for Ontario are indirect: fights over the Iran war and Pentagon policy can shape oil prices and U.S. defence and trade priorities. Watch for how a divided Washington handles tariffs and Canada talks.

stories.headline: Ford government appoints eight regional chairs, including Del Duca for York
stories.summary: Ontario named the heads of eight upper-tier councils, including former Liberal leader Steven Del Duca in York Region and outgoing Conservative MP Scott Aitchison in Muskoka, under a new law that gives them 'strong chair' powers.
stories.now: Municipal Affairs Minister Rob Flack announced the picks on Tuesday: Kevin Ashe (Durham), Ann Mulvale (Halton), Scott Aitchison (Muskoka), Frank Campion (Niagara), Nando Iannicca (Peel), Scott Davey (Waterloo), Steven Del Duca (York) and Don McIsaac as warden of Simcoe County. The province says the chairs will speed up decisions and align local priorities such as housing and infrastructure with provincial goals. Their powers include hiring or firing the chief administrative officer (the top civil servant) and department heads, directing staff, vetoing some bylaws and presenting the regional budget. Opposition critics say the move overrides local voices.
stories.backstory: Ontario first gave 'strong mayor' powers to Toronto and Ottawa in 2022 and later extended them to dozens of cities. This spring the province brought in the Better Regional Governance Act, letting it appoint chairs in Durham, Halton, Muskoka, Peel, Waterloo and York and the Simcoe warden, and cutting the size of Niagara's council. Some of these posts were previously chosen by voters or by regional councillors. The appointments come right after the Oct. 26 municipal elections.

timeline.event: Strong mayor powers for Toronto and Ottawa

stories.why: Regional governments run water, sewers, police budgets, roads and much of the planning that decides where housing goes. Appointed chairs with veto and staffing powers shift control toward Queen's Park.
stories.impact: For York, Peel, Durham and Halton residents, regional chairs now have more say over budgets that drive property taxes and over approvals for housing and infrastructure. Watch the first regional budgets under the new chairs.

stories.headline: Bank of Canada notes show oil shock drove its October rate hike
stories.summary: The central bank's summary of its Oct. 28 deliberations says officials weighed holding at 2.25% against hiking to 2.5%, and chose the hike mainly because oil prices looked set to stay high for longer.
stories.now: The Bank of Canada published its summary of Governing Council talks on Tuesday afternoon. Members considered two options, holding the policy rate at 2.25% or raising it to 2.5%, and the main reason they hiked was that oil prices tied to the Middle East war were expected to stay elevated. They also judged that stronger growth would use up spare capacity in the economy and that rising business costs would eventually show up in core inflation. Since the decision, Brent crude has fallen about 25% from its late-October peak, which could ease that worry. The next rate decision is Dec. 9.
stories.backstory: The bank cut its key rate to 2.25% in October 2025 as tariffs slowed the economy. Energy prices then surged with the Iran war, and annual inflation reached 3.1% in September, although core measures stayed near 2%. On Oct. 28 the bank raised its rate a quarter point to 2.5%, its first hike in about three years, and said further increases might be needed.
stories.why: The bank's rate sets the prime rate that variable mortgages and lines of credit follow. Its reasoning shows that falling oil prices could reduce the case for another hike.
stories.impact: GTA homeowners with variable-rate mortgages or renewing soon should watch Dec. 9. If oil keeps falling, pressure for another increase may ease; if it rebounds, borrowing costs could rise again.

stories.headline: Alaska and Mississippi Senate races stay uncalled as Democrats widen leads
stories.summary: Democrats are projected to hold at least 259 House seats and at least 54 Senate seats; in the two uncalled Senate races, Democratic challengers lead by roughly 2,500 to 2,600 votes.
stories.now: In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom led Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by 2,607 votes as of 4:30 p.m. Tuesday, a margin of about 0.27 points with roughly 97% of the vote counted, according to AP figures; independent Ty Pinkins has about 20,000 votes. Tuesday was the deadline for absentee ballots to arrive, and the state has no formal recount process, so a legal fight is possible. In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola leads Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by about 2,500 first-choice votes; with no one at 50%, the state runs its ranked-choice count on Nov. 18 and certifies on Nov. 25. NBC projects at least 259 Democratic House seats, and neither Senate race changes Democratic control.
stories.backstory: Republicans have held both chambers since January 2025, and all 435 House seats and about a third of the Senate were on the ballot. More than 53 million Americans voted early. Tariffs and high gas prices tied to the Iran war weighed on Trump's approval, and recent polls gave Democrats an edge in most key Senate races. Courts also turned back a Trump administration bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots.

timeline.event: Supreme Court rejects bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots

stories.why: Democratic control of both chambers means the administration will face subpoenas, investigations and legislative roadblocks starting in January, and trade and tariff policy could be contested in Congress.
stories.impact: Canadian exporters are watching whether a Democratic Congress moves to limit tariffs, which could ease pressure on Ontario manufacturers over time; near-term tariffs stay in place unless the White House changes them.

stories.headline: Carney to press Xi on foreign interference at APEC in Shenzhen
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney says he will tell Chinese President Xi Jinping that Canada will not accept outside meddling in its affairs when the two meet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 18–19.
stories.now: Carney said Tuesday he will use the meeting on the APEC sidelines to stress that Canada expects non-interference from China and other countries. He also plans to discuss global security and what he called a deepening economic partnership with clear guardrails. It will be his second in-person meeting with Xi this year, after a visit to China in January. Opposition critics and China watchers have questioned the shift in tone from the 2025 election campaign, when Carney named China as Canada's top geopolitical threat. Beijing has long denied interfering in Canadian politics.
stories.backstory: A federal public inquiry found that China was the most active foreign state trying to interfere in Canada's democratic institutions. Relations soured for years over arrests, tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles and Chinese duties on Canadian canola. Carney's government has since sought to rebuild trade ties with Beijing as tariffs from the Trump administration hit Canadian exports, which drew a tariff threat from Trump over any Canada-China deal.

timeline.event: Carney calls China Canada's top geopolitical threat
Carney and Xi meet at APEC in South Korea

stories.why: China is Canada's second-largest trading partner, and how Ottawa balances trade with Beijing against security worries and pressure from Washington affects farmers, automakers and diaspora communities.
stories.impact: GTA residents with family or business ties to China are among those most exposed to interference concerns. Any trade easing could matter for Ontario exporters and for car buyers, while friction with the U.S. over China ties could complicate Canada-U.S. trade talks.

stories.headline: Russia-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi 'very productive,' says Rubio
stories.summary: U.S.-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine ran about four hours in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and resume Wednesday; Rubio praised them and said Europe should eventually join.
stories.now: Russian and Ukrainian delegations met for nearly four hours Tuesday with U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the first trilateral round since February's talks in Geneva. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking from the G7 foreign ministers' meeting in Paris, called the session very productive and said European partners should eventually be part of the process. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it constructive and substantive. Germany's foreign minister said there can be no solution without Europe and urged Moscow to drop its maximalist demands. A second day of talks is set for Wednesday; no breakthrough is expected right away.
stories.backstory: U.S.-mediated efforts to end the war stalled for months while Washington focused on Iran. Rubio said in May that the effort had stagnated. Europe has repeatedly asked to be included in any deal affecting its own security.

stories.why: A deal, or a breakdown, would shape European security and Canada's allied commitments. Disagreement between the U.S. and Europe is also a risk.
stories.impact: Peace progress could ease energy and grain prices over time. Canada, a NATO and G7 member, would feel the effects of any change in security arrangements.

stories.headline: Republicans pick Jim Jordan to lead House minority; Thune keeps Senate post
stories.summary: House Republicans chose Trump ally Jim Jordan over Steve Scalise as their leader for the next Congress, and Senate Republicans re-elected John Thune after conservatives failed to delay the vote.
stories.now: In a closed-door vote Tuesday, House Republicans elected Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan as minority leader, defeating Majority Leader Steve Scalise about 106-73, according to reports. Speaker Mike Johnson had said the day after the election that he would not seek the job. In the Senate, Ron Johnson, Rick Scott and Mike Lee pushed to postpone the leadership vote so the caucus could first discuss its midterm losses, and the meeting was paused for several hours. Thune was then re-elected leader by acclamation, with no challenger, his spokesperson said. Both will lead their parties in the minority once Democrats take over in January.
stories.backstory: Republicans lost more than 40 House seats and at least seven Senate seats in the Nov. 3 midterms. Jordan co-founded the hard-right House Freedom Caucus and lost a bid for Speaker in October 2023. Thune became Senate majority leader in January 2025, succeeding Mitch McConnell.

timeline.event: Mike Johnson says he will not run for leader

stories.why: These leaders will decide how Republicans respond to Democratic investigations, budget fights and any push to limit Trump's tariffs.
stories.impact: A harder-line House minority under Jordan could make bipartisan deals, including on trade with Canada, harder to reach before the 2028 election cycle.

stories.headline: Experts warn Ford's Bill 140 would gut Ontario's Environmental Bill of Rights
stories.summary: Environmental lawyers and advocacy groups say the Ford government's Building Ontario Faster Act would strip key public rights to comment on and challenge environmental decisions; public comments close Nov. 26.
stories.now: Bill 140, the Building Ontario Faster Act, 2026, was tabled on Oct. 27 and would amend 23 laws and create two new ones. Critics focus on Schedule 8, which rewrites the Environmental Bill of Rights (EBR); Richard Lindgren of the Canadian Environmental Law Association (CELA) says the law would keep its name but lose the legal rights people actually use. Groups including Environmental Defence say it would weaken public consultation, remove appeal rights and drop some notices from the Environmental Registry of Ontario. The bill also changes the Environmental Assessment Act and the Environmental Protection Act. The province has said the changes are meant to speed up housing and infrastructure.
stories.backstory: Ontario's EBR, passed in 1993, lets residents comment on proposed environmental decisions and, in some cases, seek leave to appeal permits. The Ford government has repeatedly moved to fast-track projects, including 2025's Bill 5, which weakened species-at-risk protections and allowed special economic zones. It also exempted the proposed Dresden landfill from a full environmental assessment, a move local councils still oppose.

timeline.event: Dresden landfill exempted from full assessment

stories.why: The bill would decide how much say residents have over landfills, quarries, highways and industrial permits near their homes. Supporters say faster approvals help build housing; critics say they shut the public out.
stories.impact: GTA residents near proposed developments, aggregate pits or waste sites may have fewer ways to object or appeal. You can still comment on the Environmental Registry of Ontario until Nov. 26.

stories.headline: Toronto freezes most hiring as it faces a $1.1-billion budget gap
stories.summary: With Premier Ford ruling out a second 'New Deal', Toronto has paused most hiring to start closing a projected $1.1-billion shortfall in its 2027 budget.
stories.now: Mayor Olivia Chow confirmed on Nov. 6 that the city has frozen most hiring, exempting essential roles such as paramedics and firefighters; recruitments without an offer already made are halted, and no end date has been set. City documents suggest the 2027 gap could grow by nearly $500 million, and the TTC estimates the end of provincial funding leaves it about $379 million short next year. Ford said on Nov. 4 that the province is in tough times and will not sign a new funding deal; Chow says she will keep negotiating piece by piece. The city is also doing a line-by-line review of spending.
stories.backstory: In 2023 Toronto faced a large budget hole. Ford and Chow agreed a package that included the province taking over the Gardiner Expressway and Don Valley Parkway, with roughly $1.2 billion over three years. That deal is now winding down, and the city has been seeking more help.

stories.why: Toronto relies heavily on property taxes and fees, so a lack of new provincial or federal money keeps pressure on city budgets.
stories.impact: Toronto residents could face higher property taxes, TTC fares or service pressure in the next city budget if no new money arrives.

stories.headline: Carney government's second budget projects $62.3B deficit with $142B in new spending
stories.summary: Finance Minister Champagne tabled the budget Thursday: a $62.3-billion deficit for 2026-27 and about $142 billion in new spending over five years.
stories.now: The budget projects a $62.3-billion deficit for 2026-27, reported as down from $65.3 billion in the spring forecast, with deficits above $50 billion in each of the next four years. It adds roughly $142.1 billion in new spending over five years, much of it classed as capital spending. Debt interest is projected to reach about $85.5 billion a year by the end of the decade. Commentators are split between those who call it fiscally measured for bond markets and those who say it borrows too much. The Liberals still need opposition support in the House of Commons to pass it. The immigration levels update was expected alongside it; details were not confirmed in this run. Coverage also highlights a plan to end homelessness in Canada within ten years, focused on transitional housing and work with the provinces, and spending meant to strengthen economic and cultural sovereignty, paid for in part by an oil-revenue windfall.
stories.backstory: Champagne announced the Nov. 5 date on Oct. 20. The budget arrives while U.S. tariffs remain in place and the Bank of Canada has just raised its rate to 2.50%, its first hike since 2023.

stories.why: The budget sets Ottawa's response to tariffs, deficits and defence spending, and the immigration targets shape population growth. Budget numbers were taken from headlines and secondary reports and should be checked against the Department of Finance.
stories.impact: Watch for small-business tax changes, the deficit figure and immigration targets, which affect GTA hiring, rents and housing demand.

stories.headline: Thousands of Ontario students walk out over OSAP cuts: 'We can't afford rent'
stories.summary: Thousands of students walked out over OSAP changes and tuition, while a separate freeze on student aid at career colleges drags on with no restart date.
stories.now: On Tuesday Premier Doug Ford brushed off last week's student protests, suggesting the hundreds of demonstrators had been swayed by social media and defending his government's record on colleges and universities. Students walked out at campuses across Ontario on Nov. 5, including a large protest at the University of Toronto, over OSAP changes and tuition costs. Separately, OSAP payments to private career colleges remain frozen while KPMG auditors review them; Ford said lower-risk schools will be cleared first but gave no timeline, and Advanced Education Minister Nolan Quinn expects a new approval process in the new year. Preliminary audit concerns about student verification were referred to the OPP.
stories.backstory: OSAP is Ontario's student loan and grant program. The province froze aid to career colleges while auditors review how funds were used, and recent changes to the program and tuition rules have sparked campus protests. Students and compliant colleges say the blanket pause hurts those who did nothing wrong.

stories.impact: Students at career colleges may face delays to aid, and others should check their OSAP offer and campus fee notices for the coming terms.

stories.headline: Canada extends tariff relief program beyond U.S. steel imports
stories.summary: Ottawa widened its tariff relief program so more imported goods qualify, including goods used by public education entities and those mandated by Indigenous organizations.
stories.now: Global News reports the federal government extended its tariff relief program beyond U.S. steel imports. Goods used by public education entities, including those mandated by Indigenous organizations, will also be eligible for relief.
stories.backstory: Canada has used remission and relief measures to soften the cost of counter-tariffs on its own importers. A recent Finance Canada report found Ottawa approved about $5.6 billion in relief against a projected $2.2 billion, with more than 800 requests still unresolved.

stories.why: Counter-tariffs raise costs for Canadian buyers, so relief rules decide who pays more.
stories.impact: Schools and some public bodies in Ontario may face lower costs on imported goods. Businesses importing affected goods may be able to apply for relief.
